Chapter 7. The Search for Accountability.
When stories of abuse and torture started surfacing in the media, the whole country was forced to ask some tough questions. Who was really responsible? And how could things have gone so wrong? The truth, as you might guess, was far from simple.
Some officials tried to brush it off, insisting these were just isolated incidents—just a few so-called “bad apples.” So, investigations kicked off, and a handful of lower-ranking soldiers ended up on trial. All the while, the public was glued to shocking photos and gut-wrenching testimonies—images of hooded prisoners, accounts of humiliation and pain. People were outraged, but also confused. Was this really what America stood for?
Behind the scenes, the hunt for accountability hit roadblocks everywhere—thanks to politics and endless bureaucracy. Policies were written in such vague language that almost anyone could interpret them however they wanted. Orders were often given verbally, leaving almost no paper trail. So, when investigators tried to trace orders up the chain of command, they ran into a maze: denials, missing documents, shifting stories at every turn.
Imagine being an officer who tries to report abuse in your own unit. That’s exactly what happened to one man. Instead of being heard, his superiors dismissed his concerns, telling him he was exaggerating or misunderstood. When he wouldn’t back down, they simply reassigned him. His career stalled. The message was loud and clear—speaking out wasn’t just risky, it could cost you everything.
For many involved, the sense of betrayal ran deep. They’d trusted the system, believed in their leaders, and followed orders—only to feel abandoned and scapegoated for decisions made by those way above their heads. The idea of justice suddenly felt pretty hollow.
Most people don’t realize just how hard it is to hold powerful institutions accountable. Government machinery moves at a snail’s pace, and those in charge are experts at protecting themselves. The real truth often gets buried under layers of secrecy and spin.
But here’s the thing—some people refused to give up. Journalists, lawyers, and activists kept digging, pushing for answers, demanding transparency and real reform. Because of their efforts, there were some changes: new policies, better training, tighter oversight. Still, the scars lingered, for those who suffered and for those who were swept up in it all.
In the end, the search for accountability wasn’t just about handing out punishment. It was about facing the uncomfortable truth—no matter how painful—and figuring out how to build something better from the wreckage.
